climbing_route.label: Couloir to the north ridge saddle
climbing_route.notes: The broad snow-and-rock couloir seen from Lower Martins Park runs south toward the peak and gains roughly 2,100 ft to a saddle on the north ridge near 5,600 ft; parties report about three and a half hours for this section. Crampons and an axe are standard on firm morning snow. Late in the season the snow shrinks and more of the couloir is loose rock, so the character of this pitch changes markedly through the summer.

climbing_route.label: Descent to the Christie Glacier and the high col
climbing_route.notes: From the saddle, drop down loose gravelly slopes to the lower edge of the Christie Glacier. Reports describe few or no open crevasses, but the angle is steep enough that most parties rope up anyway and treat it as glacier terrain. A moat forms where the ice meets rock at the top of the glacier; in a good year it is a single easy step across to the high col, and it is the obvious thing to check before committing.

climbing_route.label: Summit block cliff above the col
climbing_route.notes: The barrier above the col is a chossy, eroded cliff band, very steep to locally overhanging, and this is the crux of the peak. Holds break; the ground below is a steep dirt gully dropping several hundred feet, so a slip here has serious consequences. The usable weakness is not fixed — one party found the expected line gone and had to force a route to the right across an extremely loose, essentially unprotectable ledge, belayed on a tight rope. Expect to fight through dense krummholz to get established above the cliff.

climbing_route.label: Southeast summit ridge
climbing_route.notes: Above the krummholz the rock improves and an enjoyable class 2-3 ridge scramble leads southeast to the 6,181 ft summit. Descent reverses the line; parties have rapped the summit-block cliff (about 50 ft) and again through the krummholz, and existing slings should not be assumed to be present. Refreezing snow in the couloir on a late return is a real hazard.

climbing_route.label: Choss slope to the notch south of the summit
climbing_route.notes: From the snowfield and small glacier remnant below the peak's south side, claw up dirt and broken rock to the notch immediately south of Degenhardt — the same notch that forms the upper crossing point of the Barrier. This is the worst rock on the route and is consistently described as marking the end of any good climbing in the area. Everything here is loose enough that a party should stay tight and out of each other's fall line, and running meltwater over the slabby sections has been reported as a slip hazard.

climbing_route.label: South ridge to the summit tower
climbing_route.notes: From the notch, follow the ridge north toward the summit over exposed but moderate ground. Route-finding matters more than difficulty: parties report traversing much too low and having to regain height. A small tower guards the final notch and is turned rather than climbed direct.

climbing_route.label: Summit blocks
climbing_route.notes: The last moves onto the roughly 7,800 ft summit are short 4th class on poor rock, with some accounts describing the finish as low fifth depending on the line taken. A rappel anchor has been noted on the south side, though the section is commonly downclimbed. Degenhardt is widely regarded as the chossiest peak in the Southern Pickets, so helmets and careful rope management on the descent matter more than the grade suggests.

climbing_route.label: Small glacier northwest of the peak
climbing_route.notes: The northwest side is reached by a small glacier tucked beneath the peak, gained from the ridge system running toward Luna. Snow travel here is reported as straightforward and kickable in good conditions, but it is glacier terrain and the surrounding ground is broken. Note that this line is documented mainly as a descent by parties traversing the Northern Pickets rather than as a commonly repeated ascent, so expect to be route-finding from first principles.

climbing_route.label: Ledges to the ridge crest
climbing_route.notes: Leave the glacier and work up dirty, ledge-broken terrain on the northwest flank to gain the west ridge crest. The rock is poor and vegetated, with few obvious anchors; parties descending this ground have found it slow and awkward rather than technically hard. Route-finding through the ledge bands is the real difficulty and a wrong tier can cliff you out.

climbing_route.label: Ascending traverse and summit chute
climbing_route.notes: From the crest, an ascending traverse east across loose rock leads into a chute that tops out slightly east of the summit. Everything on this upper section is described as choss, including shockingly mobile large talus on the summit ridges of the massif generally. Retreat is the concern that dominates: this is one of the most remote summits in the range, the rock takes gear poorly, and there is no quick way off.

climbing_route.label: Col east of Mystery
climbing_route.notes: From camps around 6,200 ft in Deception Basin, drop west to about 6,000 ft and climb a stagnant glacier remnant to the col east of the peak at roughly 6,700 ft. Loose scree on the descent into the basin and again below the col; the ice here is small and largely dormant but still carries a moat at its margins that grows through the season.

climbing_route.label: Snow slopes above the col
climbing_route.notes: From the col, traverse mixed rock and snow to reach open snow about 200 ft south of the col, then climb those slopes staying south of the blocky rock band immediately above. Snow angles reach around 40 degrees and take pickets well. The gullies feeding this section are the rockfall problem on the route — accounts recommend moving one at a time and keeping the party to three or fewer.

climbing_route.label: Notch at about 7,500 ft
climbing_route.notes: A short 4th class step on poor rock, with steep runout dirt below it, gains a notch near 7,500 ft; the common advice is to trend climber's left on the approach to it. This is the commitment point — it has to be downclimbed on the way out, usually unroped, and one party rated a single move on the reverse at 5.8. A moat over 30 ft deep has been reported below the gully late in the season, which can change how this section is entered and exited.

climbing_route.label: Summit gully and block
climbing_route.notes: Beyond the notch a clean class 3 gully leads to the summit block, where the rock is markedly better than anything below and the line to the 7,639 ft top is obvious. Some accounts give the peak an overall class 3 rating by the easiest line, with the 4th class step being the deciding feature; unavoidable loose rock, scree and dirt with exposure characterize the whole ascent regardless of which numbers are quoted.

climbing_route.label: Glacier crossing and start of the face
climbing_route.notes: The wall is accessed from its west side after crossing the glacier remnant beneath it, and the start is just left of the snowfield at the bottom of the face. Third and fourth class scrambling on comparatively solid rock leads up to and above that snowpatch. The ice below is small but broken and mostly unbridged by mid-season, so it is treated as glacier travel; the moat where snow meets rock at the base is the usual obstacle.

climbing_route.label: Lower face rising traverse
climbing_route.notes: Long, mostly third class pitches climb above the snowfield while traversing steadily rightward. The route takes the right, or western, of the two ribs that split the north face. Parties simul-climb much of this. The main risk here is not difficulty but committing to the wrong rib — the line is defined by where you exit at the top, and the face is over 2,000 ft tall with limited options to reverse.

climbing_route.label: Dihedrals to the buttress crest
climbing_route.notes: The ascending traverse steepens and follows dihedrals and cracks, aiming for the right or western crest of the buttress about two thirds of the way up the lower face, identifiable by the rock darkening. A sharp prow marks roughly the lower third of the buttress. Time on the crest itself is brief and reported as no harder than 5.7 on generally clean, solid rock.

climbing_route.label: Chimney back on the face
climbing_route.notes: Move back left off the crest onto the face and aim for a chimney above an awkward belay. Reported difficulty here varies with the exact line: some parties keep it to about 5.4, while a variation that traverses further right lower down and takes the true buttress hits a 5.8 traverse crux near the top of the chimney. Upper pitches on this part of the wall have been described as 5.7 to 5.8 on good rock, with the route as a whole graded around III-IV, 5.8.

climbing_route.label: Snow finger, exposed crest and the summits
climbing_route.notes: The long snow finger on the upper face forms a ramp that carries the route for a good distance; carry what you need to climb it. Above its top, the climbing turns to scrambling on a wildly exposed ridge crest, then a traverse around a small tower to the notch between the false and true summits. The false summit is taken directly on an exposed easy fifth class hand traverse, then downclimbed before the short climb to the true 8,151 ft top. Rock quality deteriorates near the top, with steep, extremely loose ground reported; a fatal-consequence rockfall accident on this buttress involved a sizeable block that had appeared solid tearing loose. Descent is normally the West Ridge gully. This is one of the longest and most committing lines in the range and retreat from high on it is genuinely difficult.

climbing_route.label: Neve Glacier crossing
climbing_route.notes: A short snow climb from camp gains the Colonial-Neve col, then the route crosses the broad Neve Glacier toward the ridge just west of the summit. Crevasses are generally modest in number but present and open more as the season goes on, so parties rope and carry glacier gear. It is a long crossing and the last of it is where the ice meets rock, which is where a moat or schrund forms late season.

climbing_route.label: Gully onto the west ridge
climbing_route.notes: Around 8,200 ft leave the snow and traverse left roughly 100 ft into an obvious northwest-facing gully, then scramble up it about 50 to 100 ft. This gully holds snow, rime and verglas well into early July, and parties have had to climb over its left edge and drop onto a ramp system that was also iced. It is the section where footing, not difficulty, decides how the day goes.

climbing_route.label: Arete and north-side ledges to the notch
climbing_route.notes: Traverse left onto an arete and climb it about 75 ft, traverse left again, then up the north side roughly 150 ft to the notch between a pinnacle and the summit. A couple of 4th class moves at the notch move out onto the south side directly above a deep gully — short, but the most exposed position on the peak. Short-roping through here is common when the ridge is airy or holding ice.

climbing_route.label: South-side summit gully
climbing_route.notes: From the notch, up the ridge about 20 ft, then traverse right on ledges to a gully on the south side of the summit; the gully is easy and about 150 ft to the top, and it downclimbs readily. Route-finding is the trap rather than the climbing: reports agree the last 100 vertical feet run class 3 to class 4 if you find the ledges and can be pushed to class 5 if you do not, and all options off the correct line look steeper and higher-consequence.

climbing_route.label: Moat and the toe of the buttress
climbing_route.notes: Cross the Colchuck Glacier on its true-right margin in crampons to reach the lowest point of the buttress. The moat where snow meets rock is the variable here — it can be a step across a snow bridge or block in a good year and the technical crux of the day in a lean one, and parties do rope for it. There is no water above the lake, and the rock start is where the day's timing is decided.

climbing_route.label: Lower buttress pitches
climbing_route.notes: The lower section, most commonly climbed by the left-hand start, takes wide broken cracks on solid rock to gain the crest below a large headwall. Above that, downclimb about 15 ft off the crest and work up and right on ramps to a vertical seam, then back left to a ledge at around 5.7. The pitch into the main dihedral includes a shallow chimney at 5.7 to 5.8 and is the dirtiest part of the route — moss, loose gravel and old fixed pins marking the way. Two established starts exist and mixing them up is the usual route-finding error.

climbing_route.label: Rising ledge traverse
climbing_route.notes: A long rising traverse on ledge systems at roughly 5.0 to 5.5 links several pitches. Rock quality improves through this section and most parties simul-climb or move together in approach shoes to save time; on a 14-pitch route this is where the schedule is made up. Loose debris on the ledges is the hazard for anyone below.

climbing_route.label: Crux corner to the ridge crest
climbing_route.notes: The route's technical crux climbs the wall above the ledges, meandering left before traversing back right into a left-facing corner that is run to the ridge crest, generally reported at 5.8 to 5.9. Rock here is solid and the movement varied, but the crux involves steep, smooth climbing before a cam can be placed blind in a horizontal crack. A rack to 3 inches with doubles from about .5 to 2 is what parties report using.

climbing_route.label: Upper crest, headwall and summit
climbing_route.notes: Follow the buttress crest, then traverse right onto ledges to reach the base of the headwall at around 5.6. The final pitch traverses right roughly 80 ft under large blocks into a north-facing dihedral, finishing on blocky terrain to the summit plateau; the last move has been reported as a mantel past a loose block. Budget for nine hours or so on rock at Grade IV. Descent is the Colchuck Glacier, taking the skier's-right fork back toward the lake. Benighted parties are common — the length, not the grade, is what catches people.

climbing_route.label: Hanging snow slope to the ridge base
climbing_route.notes: The only documented ascent gained this ridge after climbing Sharkfin Tower, descending from it, and traversing a steep hanging snow slope directly to the base of the ridge. There is no established independent approach to the foot of the crest, so the snow condition on that traverse is the gatekeeper and it is committing terrain to cross in poor conditions.

climbing_route.label: A cheval section
climbing_route.notes: The distinctive feature of the ridge is two pitches climbed a cheval, straddling a crest of rock described as having the consistency of feta cheese. The ridge carries an X rating in its only published account, meaning protection is effectively absent and a fall would not be held. Nothing on this section should be trusted as an anchor.

climbing_route.label: Upper ridge to the summit
climbing_route.notes: Roughly another 1,000 ft of climbing remains above the a cheval section to reach the 8,894 ft summit, all of it on previously unclimbed and consistently chossy rock. Retreat is the defining hazard: the party that made the ascent reported the rock too poor to rappel reliably and ultimately abandoned their intended continuation of the ridge traverse, descending instead by rappels and traversing to the Quien Sabe Glacier. Beyond this single account there is no route description for the crest, and it should not be treated as a repeated or verified line.
